newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Thousands of Colombian police killed this decade.
newsitem.headline: Thousands of Colombian police killed this decade.

text.p: A total of 4,617 policemen have been killed since 1990 in Colombia, the most anywhere in the world, a senior police official said on Wednesday.

Gen. Ismael Trujillo, head of the judicial police or Dijin, said the number of police fatalities and the fact that 81 of every 100,000 Colombians was a victim of homicide or murder, underscored the "crime epidemic" that has been tearing Colombia apart for years.

"We're killing each other for the most futile and elementary things," Trujillo said, adding that rampant corruption and a weak judicial system also meant that at least 90 percent of all crimes in Colombia went unpunished.
"There's been a total loss of values," Trujillo told a seminar on violence and kidnapping at Bogota's Universidad de los Andes.
Decrying what he said was an open contempt for life, he said: "The worst of all evils in Colombia is corruption and it's the father of all our other problems."
A recent World Bank report described Colombia as the country with the highest murder rate in Latin America.
Trujillo said Colombia's death rate of 81 per 100,000 due to violence compared with 9 per 100,000 in the United States and 1 per 100,000 in Chile.

He did not elaborate on the cause of the high number of policemen killed since 1990 -- including more than 110 so far this year. But he said 1,337 "terrorist" crimes occurred in Colombia last year alone. He was referring to attacks attributed to the country's leading leftist guerrilla groups and said there had been a "tremendously worrisome" surge in guerrilla activity over the last year.
Rodrigo Villamizar, head of the government's anti-kidnapping office, told the same seminar that Colombia had the world's highest rate of abductions.
"Kidnapping has become an industry," Villamizar said, adding guerrillas alone were now abducting an average of 500 people a year.
Roughly 25 percent of the world's kidnappings occur in Colombia, Villamizar said, describing the country as awash in "debts written in blood."
